metadata.title: Tracing a Crash-Looping Backend
metadata.source: Incident 01 notes (Dev Backend Crash-Looping: Stale MONGODB_URI, week of 2026-08-25); Cloud Run request log 2026-08-27T23:29:21Z (sanitized); MEDAS login screenshot (pantry/medas-login-ui-after-fix.png)
metadata.description: A MEDAS 2.0 (pre-release) project update: the dev backend on Cloud Run returned Service Unavailable on every request, including /health. Traced through Cloud Run logs to a stale MONGODB_URI secret pointing at a terminated cluster; because init_database() runs at import time, the failed connection crashed every worker boot. Fixed with a new dev Atlas cluster under the institutional account, a new secret version picked up via :latest, and verified with /health plus a real login query.
metadata.note: Evidence handling: the dev database holds example test data only, no real patient data. Log shown in B12 is sanitized (client IP, instance ID, trace/span IDs, project ID and full service URLs removed). B04/B06 are reconstructions from the incident notes, labeled as such on screen; B08 is a labeled illustration of the pattern, not MEDAS source. Dev URLs returning 503 since 2026-09-20 is a separate billing issue and is not part of this story.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW -- Claude composer, ask shown answered; FELLOWS-SUBMISSION intro line + AI narration disclosure
beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Akshit and this video is about tracing a crash-looping backend on MEDAS, a diagnostic advising system for emergency physicians. One week in August, every request to our dev backend came back Service Unavailable. A quick note: the voice you're hearing is an AI narrator reading my script.

props.command: Our Cloud Run backend answers every request, even /health, with Service Unavailable. Where do I start?
output: Service Unavailable: the container never answered
check Cloud Run → Logs before the app code
look for a worker that boots, then dies

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW -- hesitant writer; the correction IS the misconception the body dismantles
beats.narration_text: Our backend was down because its startup needed a database that no longer existed. Not a bug in a route. One stale setting took the whole service down with it.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer typing bookend (EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW): the overview accumulates token by token, so mid-beat frames are mostly cream by design.

props.text:
Our backend was down
because of a bug in our code.

beats.role_note: what MEDAS is, before any detail
beats.narration_text: MEDAS is built with emergency medicine services. A doctor describes a case by speech or text. A super-learner of AI agents and an early sepsis predictor weigh in, and an aggregation layer merges them into one ranked list of possible diagnoses with probabilities. It's a second opinion; the doctor still decides. MEDAS 2.0 is in pre-release, and my part is the backend that carries it.

props.footerNote: An immediate second opinion for emergency physicians. An audit system records every exchange; the doctor makes the final call.
props.sparkLine: A second opinion, not a verdict.

beats.role_note: FRAMEWORK beat -- the boot path every request depends on, shown before the example
beats.narration_text: Here's the path every request depends on. Cloud Run starts a container. Gunicorn binds to port eighty-eighty. The app imports its routes, and that import calls init database, which asks MongoDB's client to resolve the cluster's address through DNS. Every link has to hold before even the health check can answer.

props.footerNote: Before /health can answer, all of this must succeed. One broken link and the worker never finishes booting.

beats.role_note: worked example begins -- reconstruction from incident notes, labeled
beats.narration_text: The symptom. Both dev URLs were live: DNS resolved, and Cloud Run showed the service as deployed. But every request, even slash health, returned Service Unavailable. That detail matters. A missing route gets you a four-oh-four from the app. This page means the container itself never answered.

props.caption: Reconstructed from incident notes. Not a 404: the app never got far enough to reply.

beats.narration_text: First suspect: a secret that was never created. In Secret Manager for the dev project, both JWT secret and MongoDB URI existed. So that was ruled out. The next stop was the one this error points to: the Cloud Run logs.

props.title: secret-manager-check.txt
props.code:
Secret Manager  (dev project)

  JWT_SECRET     exists  ✓
  MONGODB_URI    exists  ✓

→ ruled out
→ next stop: Cloud Run → Logs

beats.role_note: the crash-loop pattern -- reconstruction from incident notes, labeled
beats.narration_text: The logs showed a loop. Gunicorn starts and binds to eighty-eighty. A few seconds later the worker crashes, the worker fails to boot, and the master shuts down. Then it repeats, on every single request, because with no healthy instance Cloud Run starts a fresh one each time. At the bottom of the traceback: pymongo trying to resolve the cluster's DNS records, and failing.

props.caption: Reconstructed from incident notes. Boot, crash, repeat.

beats.role_note: the framework from B03 again, now with the broken link lit
beats.narration_text: So I opened the secret's actual value. The MongoDB URI pointed at an old cluster, a personal one from before the project consolidated onto Professor Tayyar's institutional Atlas account. That cluster had been terminated. The DNS lookup had nothing left to find, and the chain broke at its very first database call.

props.title: The chain broke at the first database call.
props.footerNote: The secret still pointed at a terminated personal cluster.

beats.role_note: labeled illustration of the import-time pattern, not MEDAS source
beats.narration_text: Why did one bad setting take down everything, even the health check? Because init database runs at module import time, before Flask can serve a single request. The failed connection doesn't break one route. It breaks the boot. No healthy worker means no response at all, and Cloud Run just tries again on the next request.

props.title: routes_pattern.py
props.code:
# ILLUSTRATION of the pattern, not MEDAS source
# user_management/routes.py  (simplified)

db = init_database()   # runs when the module is IMPORTED
                       # dead cluster -> exception
                       # -> worker fails to boot

# Flask never starts serving.
# Every route is unreachable, /health included.

beats.role_note: resolution steps from the incident notes
beats.narration_text: The fix. A new, properly owned dev cluster under the institutional Atlas account, seeded with example test data, with no real patient records. Seeding it surfaced a separate index-name issue, a story for another video. Then a new version of the MongoDB URI secret. No redeploy needed: the service reads that secret's latest version, so the next container to boot picked it up.

props.title: Update the secret; the next boot does the rest.

phases.label: Seed example data
phases.desc: test data only, no patient records

props.footerNote: Seeding surfaced a separate index-name issue, a story for another video.

beats.role_note: FALSIFIABILITY beat -- why a passing /health alone is not proof
beats.narration_text: How do you know it's actually fixed? A healthy health check only proves the process boots. It doesn't prove the database works. So the second check was a login with wrong credentials. Getting back invalid credentials means the backend looked up a user in the database and answered. That's a real query, end to end.

props.title: verification-checks.txt
props.code:
GET  /health
     -> healthy JSON
     proves: the process boots

POST /auth/login   (wrong password)
     -> {"error": "Invalid credentials"}
     proves: a real database query ran
props.sparkLine: Boots isn't the same as works.

beats.role_note: fellow's own screen capture (media/B11.png, original in pantry/) -- the working dev frontend after the fix
beats.narration_text: And the dev frontend was loading again. This is the MEDAS login screen, with its four language options, talking to the repaired backend.

beats.role_note: real Cloud Run request log, 2026-08-27, sanitized
beats.narration_text: Here's the receipt from Cloud Run's request log on August twenty-seventh: a post to auth login, status two hundred, answered in about fifty-four milliseconds by revision twelve of the dev service. A successful login, with the database behind it doing its job.

props.caption: Real log entry, sanitized: client IP, instance, trace IDs and URLs removed.

beats.role_note: the lessons from the incident notes, one page
beats.narration_text: Three lessons. Service Unavailable, not a four-oh-four, means the container itself isn't answering, so check the Cloud Run logs first. A personal database cluster was a single point of failure; every environment now lives under the institutional account. And Secret Manager's latest alias applies on the next container start, so updating a secret doesn't need a redeploy.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW -- suggested prompt, read aloud verbatim and discussed
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Here is my app's startup code. List every external service it contacts before it can answer a health check. For each one, tell me what error I'd see in the logs if it disappeared, and a request that proves it's really working. That last part matters most. It turns a vague outage into a checklist, and it tells you which check actually proves the fix.
